Learning Objectives
Specify the epidemiology of, etiology of, and risk factors for plantar fasciitis.
Perform an appropriate clinical examination for plantar fasciitis.
Understand the surgical and nonsurgical management of plantar fasciitis.

Heel pain (subcalcaneal pain syndrome) is the most common foot-related symptom
leading patients to seek medical care for their feet. It often has an atraumatic, insidious
onset and is associated with start-up pain that eases with activity and is relieved by rest.
Plantar fasciitis also may be associated with anatomic variations (eg, pes planus, pes
cavus, or excessive femoral anteversion) and may be observed in combination with a
triad of tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction, plantar fasciitis, and tarsal tunnel
syndrome has been described. Approximately 50% of patients with plantar fasciitis have
a plantar heel enthesophyte (spur), typically located in the origin of the flexor hallucis
brevis; however, heel spurs are not considered the cause of heel pain in such patients.
Epidemiology
Heel Pain/Plantar Fasciitis
Heel pain may occur at any age. The peak incidence occurs between 40 and 60 years. The
highest incidence of plantar fasciitis is in women aged 45 to 64 years.
Race and ethnicity play no role in this entity.
Stress fractures are more common in women than men; they also are more common in
military recruits than the general population.
Risk factors include limited ankle dorsiflexion because of tightness of the Achilles tendon or
isolated gastrocnemius contracture,1 obesity (body mass index >30 kg/m2), and prolonged
weight bearing (Resources 1 and 2).
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Anatomy
Subcutaneous tendon–like structure extending from the calcaneus to the toes

Anatomy
The plantar fascia is a strong, subcutaneous aponeurosis on the plantar foot extending
from the calcaneus to the toes. It is composed of collagen and elastic fibers that share
histologic and mechanical traits with tendons and ligaments and not with fascia.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:49 PM
AAOS | Plantar Fasciitis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000008
2/23

Originating from the plantar calcaneus tuberosity, the plantar fascia extends distally to
the toes, inserting through a complex network that incorporates the
metatarsophalangeal joints and the flexor tendon sheaths. Although it is composed of
three bands (central, lateral, and medial), the major portion of the plantar fascia is the
central component2 (Figure 1). 
Figure 1 Schematic drawings of a foot and ankle show the anatomy of the tibial nerve in
the tarsal tunnel before (A) and after (B) release of the flexor retinaculum (laciniate
ligament), plantar fascia, abductor hallucis, and flexor digitorum brevis. (Reproduced
with permission from Gould JS: Tarsal tunnel syndrome. Foot Ankle Clin 2011;16[2]:275-
286.)
Biomechanics
Supports the longitudinal arch of the foot via a windlass mechanism

Biomechanics
The plantar fascia serves primarily to support the medial longitudinal arch of the foot.
During standing, the weight of the body is supported almost entirely by the passive
structures of the foot, including the plantar fascia. At the end of the stance phase, the
toes dorsiflex, and the plantar fascia assumes a dynamic function. Specifically, increased
tension on the plantar fascia creates a windlass effect, stiffening the arch and assisting in
raising the longitudinal arch to create a more rigid lever for push-off2 (Figure 2).

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000008

Figure 2 Clinical photograph of a bone model of the foot and ankle show the windlass
mechanism. A truss is superimposed over the bone model. As the toes dorsiflex, the
drum (metatarsophalangeal joints) rotates, applying tension to the tie rod (plantar fascia)
and effectively supporting the arch. (Reproduced with permission from de Asla RJ:
Anatomy and biomechanics of the foot and ankle, in Thordarson DB, ed: Orthopaedic
Surgery Essentials: Foot and Ankle, ed 2. Philadelphia, PA, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins,
2012.)
Etiology
Pathogenesis likely is a result of a combination of microtrauma near the calcaneal insertion
exacerbated by gastrocnemius or combined gastrocnemius-soleus contractures increasing
tensile forces.

Etiology
The etiology of plantar fasciitis is unclear but likely entails repetitive microtrauma to the
plantar fascia causing microtears and periostitis. This occurs in a relative hypovascular
region near the insertion on the calcaneus. In addition, isolated contracture of the
gastrocnemius muscle or a contracture of the gastrocnemius-soleus complex is
theorized to contribute to overload and inflammation in the plantar fascia.1,3,4 Tightness
at the Achilles tendon from gastrocnemius contracture leads to increased strain on the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:49 PM
AAOS | Plantar Fasciitis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000008
4/23

tension side of the plantar foot, particularly at the plantar fascia, which can break down
near its insertion at the plantar medial calcaneus.
Natural History
Plantar fasciitis often results from an increase in activity related to weight bearing or a change
in running shoes or other types of shoes. Occasionally, symptoms arise spontaneously. Plantar
fasciitis resolves without surgery in more than 90% of patients.
Risk Factors
Women aged 45 to 64 years have the highest incidence of plantar fasciitis.
Risk factors include limited ankle dorsiflexion because of tightness of the Achilles tendon or
isolated gastrocnemius contracture, obesity (body mass index >30 kg/m2), and prolonged
weight bearing.
May be associated with anatomic variations (eg, pes planus, pes cavus, or excessive femoral
anteversion)
Although 50% of patients with plantar fasciitis have a plantar heel spur (located in the flexor
hallucis brevis), heel spurs are not thought to be pain generators.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
The patient history and physical examination are extremely important in evaluating heel pain
because imaging and laboratory studies may be of limited value.
Patient History
A patient with plantar fasciitis most often will report start-up inferior heel pain (eg, in the
morning or after sitting for an extended time) and may prefer to walk on the toes for the first
few steps.
The pain usually lessens with ambulation and increases with activity, especially on hard
surfaces.
Physical Examination
SEND FEEDBACK

AAOS | Plantar Fasciitis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000008
5/23

The foot should be examined for the point of maximal tenderness (Figure 3).
A traumatic tear of the plantar fascia may occur in the midfoot region. Patients in whom this
finding is noted may have decreased tension of the plantar fascia. The decreased tension can
be detected by dorsiflexing the hallux with one hand while palpating the plantar fascia with the
other hand.
In patients with plantar fasciitis, the point of maximal tenderness typically is located at the
proximal medial origin of the plantar fascia (Figure 3).
Palpation of the plantar fascia with the toes and ankle in dorsiflexion increases the plantar
fascia tension and, therefore, the sensitivity of the examination.
The leg and ankle should be examined for a gastrocnemius contracture, noted as a positive
Silfverskiöld test5 (Figure 4)
Figure 3 Clinical photograph of a foot shows the points of maximal tenderness in relation to the
most common causes of heel pain. The foot is shown with the toes to the right and the medial
aspect of the foot and ankle at the top. (Reproduced with permission from Richardson DR,
Richardson EG: Heel pain, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1197-1203.)

Figure 4 Photographs of a leg show the Silfverskiöld test. A, An equinus contracture with the
knee in extension denoted by the angle formed by the tibia and the plantar aspect of the foot
(black lines). B, Dorsiflexion past neutral with 90° of flexion of the knee, denoting an isolated
gastrocnemius contracture. (Reproduced from Patel MS, Kadakia AR: Metatarsalgia, in Chou LB,
ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Foot and Ankle, ed 6. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 215-227.)
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Weight-bearing lateral and axial radiographs of the hindfoot may be used to assess arthritic
changes, structural abnormalities, or bony pathology. They are not necessary on the initial
visit.
Enthesophytes may be observed on the plantar heel on lateral radiographs.
Computed Tomography
Usually, CT is not necessary unless evaluating for arthritis or neoplasm.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (Figure 5)
Although usually not necessary, MRI may show chronic inflammatory changes and interstitial
tearing at the plantar fascia origin. It also may aid ruling out other conditions, such as tarsal
tunnel masses and calcaneal stress fractures.

Figure 5 Lateral radiograph of the foot of a patient with heel pain demonstrates a large heel spur
emanating from the distal plantar calcaneal tuberosity (black arrow). Several small soft-tissue
calcifications are distal to the heel spur (white arrow). These calcifications may represent
dystrophic calcification within a degenerative plantar fascia ligament or an acute fracture of a
preexisting heel spur. The bony anatomy of the calcaneus is otherwise unremarkable.
(Reproduced from Frey C: Heel spur, in Johnson TR, Steinbach LS, eds: Essentials of Musculoskeletal
Imaging. Rosemont, IL. American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2004, pp 565-568.)

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
The plantar fascia can be visualized on coronal and sagittal MRIs and will be thickened to
approximately 8 mm. Increased signal intensity is observed on short tau inversion
recovery and T2-weighted MRIs and may spread to the adjoining calcaneus at the
insertion site. This is thought to represent reactive edema within the bone (Figure 6).
Figure 6 MRIs of a foot with plantar fasciitis. A, T1-weighted sagittal MRI shows
thickened, deep plantar fascia at its insertion onto the calcaneus (arrow). Abnormal

tau inversion recovery MRI shows an abnormally high signal intensity about the deep
plantar fascia (arrow). (Reproduced from Recht MP, Donley BG. Magnetic resonance
imaging of the foot and ankle. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2001;9[3]:187-199.)
Other
A bone scan typically is not performed but may help quantitate inflammation and guide
management (Figure 7).
Laboratory studies are not necessary unless other etiologies are suspected (eg, inflammatory
arthritis, infection).
Figure 7 Bone scan of the foot of a patient with proximal plantar fasciitis shows tracer uptake at
the plantar aspect of the calcaneus (arrow), which suggests focal inflammation at the plantar
fascia origin on the calcaneus. Note that no changes are present within the body of the
calcaneus, ruling out a stress fracture of the tuberosity. (Reproduced from Frey C: Heel spur, in
Johnson TR, Steinbach LS, eds: Essentials of Musculoskeletal Imaging. Rosemont, IL. American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2004, pp 565-568.)

Pathology
The pathology is characterized primarily by tissue degeneration (fasciosis) with secondary
inflammation.
An infiltration of macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells cause tissue destruction. If the
insult continues and the reparative process is unable to keep up, then immature
vascularization and fibrosis develop. The fascia usually is thickened and gritty, with loss of
elasticity and increased stiffness (which may play a role in continued symptoms and decrease
blood flow to the area).
After being damaged, the biologic and biomechanical properties of the involved connective
tissue may never be completely restored because of its relative hypovascularity.
Diagnosis
Primarily via patient history and clinical examination findings
Differential diagnosis
Plantar fasciitis is the most common cause of heel pain.
Calcaneal stress fracture, entrapment of the first branch of the lateral plantar nerve (which
innervates the abductor digiti quinti), and fat pad atrophy also should be high on the list of
differential diagnoses. Occasionally, tarsal tunnel syndrome may cause heel pain.
A high index of suspicion is necessary to diagnose the less common causes of heel pain
syndrome, such as tumor or infection.
Heel pain in the older adults and patients with an atypical presentation should be
investigated to rule out insufficiency fractures and tumors.

Diagnosis
Weight-bearing radiographs play a role in evaluating other causes of pain and
assessing the structural integrity of the foot; however, a diagnosis of plantar fasciitis is
based primarily on patient history and physical examination findings. Patients
typically will report start-up plantar heel pain. On physical examination, this is
associated with tenderness at the plantar medial heel and, often, tightness in the
gastrocnemius, as demonstrated by a positive Silfverskiöld test result.

Differential Diagnosis
Plantar fascia rupture
Fat pad atrophy
Fat pad contusion
Calcaneal stress fracture
Entrapment of the first branch of the lateral plantar nerve
Calcaneal apophysitis (Sever disease)
Tumor (eg, osteoid osteoma)
Tarsal tunnel syndrome
Gout or other inflammatory arthropathies (eg, spondyloarthropathy, such as ankylosing
spondylopathy)
Infection
Radiculopathy
Paget disease
Neuropathy
Foreign body reaction
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Techniques/Procedures
Calf and Achilles tendon stretching
Night splints and orthoses
NSAIDs are commonly used; however, little evidence supports their use
Corticosteroid injections
Alternative therapies

Techniques/Procedures
Initial management of plantar fasciitis should include stretching, patient education,
activity modifications, and consideration of orthotic use. Stretching is the mainstay of
nonsurgical treatment in patients with plantar fasciitis.6-13 Plantar fascia–specific
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:49 PM
AAOS | Plantar Fasciitis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000008
11/23

stretching is critical. Regardless, stretching the Achilles tendon, calf muscles, and
hamstring muscles (components of the posterior kinetic chain) also should be
encouraged.14-17 A non–weight-bearing, plantar fascia–specific stretching exercise
program (Figure 8) in combination with calf and Achilles tendon stretching has been
reported to be more effective than the traditional program of isolated Achilles tendon
stretching exercises (Figure 9).
Night splints may be an effective adjunct to stretching.18 These serve to stretch the calf
and the plantar fascia while the patient is asleep. Little evidence demonstrates the
effectiveness of custom or prefabricated orthoses; however, custom orthoses have no
benefit over prefabricated devices.19
Corticosteroid injection is accepted as the initial invasive treatment option in the
management of plantar fasciitis in patients in whom other nonsurgical treatment
options fail. Corticosteroid injection may provide temporary relief of pain and may be
more effective if performed under ultrasonographic guidance. Corticosteroid injections
have been proven to be useful, but they also may result in adverse effects.20-24 A 2.4%
rate of rupture is associated with corticosteroid injections.23 Other potential adverse
effects include postinjection flare, facial flushing, skin atrophy, and fat pad atrophy.24
The FDA has approved the use of electrohydraulic and electromagnetic extracorporeal
shock wave therapy for the management of recalcitrant chronic plantar heel pain that
lasts more than 6 months. Several studies supporting its use have reported short- and
long-term improvements in pain reduction and increased function.25
Interest is increasing in orthobiologics (eg, platelet-rich plasma, bone marrow aspirate
concentrate, amniotic membrane injections) and botulinum toxin injections. These
treatment options may not be approved by the FDA. Platelet-rich plasma injection is
supported by evidence. The evidence suggests that platelet-rich plasma injections may
be as effective as a fasciotomy and, compared with other nonsurgical treatment options,
may offer additional benefit, including increased benefit over corticosteroid injections.
Results are limited because of the high degree of heterogeneity in the studies.26-31.

Surgical Management
Indications
Surgical management is indicated for recalcitrant pain that interferes with activities of daily
living. The length of nonsurgical management may vary by provider; however, the American
Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society stated that nonsurgical management should be attempted
for a minimum of 6 to 12 months before surgical management is considered.32
Contraindications
Absolute contraindications: vascular insufficiency, active infection
Relative contraindications: history of hypersensitivity, complex regional pain syndrome,
smoking, obesity, and concomitant medical conditions potentially contributing to the pain (eg,
neuropathy, fibromyalgia)
Techniques/Procedures
Primary surgical treatment options are open versus endoscopic plantar fasciotomy or
gastrocnemius recession.
Evidence suggests that gastrocnemius recession is equal to or even more effective than open
partial plantar fasciotomy.33,34
Gastrocnemius Recession
A Strayer procedure can be performed open or endoscopically.
The incision is either posterior or posteromedial, the fascia is opened, and the gastrocnemius
aponeurosis is incised at the myotendinous junction transversely as the ankle is brought into
plantar flexion. The aponeurosis should separate approximately 10 mm, and the soleus should
be observed at the base.
The sural nerve is protected to minimize postoperative neuralgia.
The soleus is protected to minimize weakness.
The crural fascia is closed as a separate layer (Figure 10).
Postoperative management varies by surgeon but typically involves immediate–weight bearing
in orthoses for 2 weeks followed by physical therapy for strengthening exercises.
Potential complications include postoperative weakness, scarring, and sural nerve injury.

Division of the plantaris tendon. B, Exposure and elevation of the sural nerve off the posterior


Gastrocnemius Recession
Gastrocnemius recession can be performed at different levels. Typically, the more
cephalad the surgery, less release of the contracture will be necessary with less
postoperative weakness. Proximal, isolated medial gastrocnemius release is performed
in the popliteal fossa because the fascia is released from the medial femoral condyle. A
Baumann rerelease is performed at the anterior fascia of the gastrocnemius
approximately midway along the muscle. Distal release, commonly known as a Stayer
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:49 PM
AAOS | Plantar Fasciitis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000008
15/23

procedure, is performed at the posterior portion at the level of the myotendinous
junction of the gastrocnemius muscle.
Outcomes
Effective in the management of recalcitrant plantar fasciitis pain
Plantar flexion weakness is a complication.

Outcomes
Gastrocnemius recession has been shown to be effective based on the premise that
equinus contracture often is associated with plantar fasciitis1,4,33,35-38 Results measured
by visual analog scale scores and improved function according to patient-reported
functional improvement demonstrate positive outcomes.35-37 Overall, patient
satisfaction ranges from 81% to 93%.34,39 Postoperative weakness is questionable, with
evidence showing no negative gait adaptations and no substantial loss of strength 3
months after isolated gastrocnemius recession.40,41 Improvement in strength has been
demonstrated after isolated proximal medial gastrocnemius recession.42
Some studies have demonstrated that endoscopic gastrocnemius recession minimizes
incisional risks while resulting in adequate release; however, evidence is
inconclusive.43,44
Plantar Fasciotomy
The medial one-third to two-thirds of the plantar fascia is incised via an open or endoscopic
approach (Video 1). Endoscopic procedures have been shown to be more effective with a
faster recovery and superior short-term outcomes compared with mini-open or open
procedures, with similar long-term results and patient satisfaction.45-47
In patients with evidence of plantar fasciitis and compression neuropathy, an open procedure
must be performed. This procedure consists of distal tarsal tunnel decompression and partial
plantar fascia release (normally one-quarter of the medial band). Consideration must be given
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:49 PM
AAOS | Plantar Fasciitis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000008
16/23

to releasing the adductor hallucis fascia and the first branch of the lateral plantar nerve.
Although the plantar calcaneal tuberosity osteophyte (heel spur) is unrelated to plantar
fasciitis, the osteophyte usually is removed at the time of surgery.
Postoperative management typically involves a period of protected–weight bearing and
immobilization, with progression to a normal shoe within 2 to 6 weeks postoperatively
Potential complications include damage to the lateral plantar nerve, complete fascia rupture
with resultant loss of the medial longitudinal arch, stress reaction of the dorsolateral midfoot,
and continued pain.33,48,49 Theoretically, an endoscopic approach results in fewer wound
complications, earlier weight bearing, and earlier return to activity; however, lateral plantar
nerve injury rates may be higher with endoscopic techniques, and complete (rather than
partial) transection of the plantar fascia may be an unintended consequence of an endoscopic
technique.
